metadata.title: Understanding the relationships among ICT use, self-efficacy, and achievement in PISA 2022: A multigroup analysis featuring gender and immigrant status

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses Finnish student microdata from PISA 2022 and follows OECD guidance for analyzing PISA, including accounting for the complex sampling design and measurement error. The authors state that they used all student weights and all replication weights, and they implement Fay’s balanced repeated replication (BRR) with a factor of 0.5 and 80 replication weights. Achievement-related analyses are conducted with 10 plausible values per subject, and model fit and mediation effects are computed using PV-averaged results across all 10 plausible values. For immigrant-status grouping, the analytic sample is reduced because immigrant status is derived from country of birth and both parents’ information; students with missing responses for these items are assigned no valid immigrant value, leading to smaller group Ns.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports how plausible values are handled (10 PVs with Fay’s BRR and PV-averaged mediation/model-fit reporting), but it does not explicitly describe a missing-data method for the PVs or other variables beyond the immigrant-status derivation rule. Because the immigrant grouping is reduced due to missing immigrant-status inputs, missingness handling is partially addressed by exclusion for that derived variable, yet the authors do not provide a general missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise/pairwise deletion rules across all variables). This is a reporting gap for missingness beyond the immigrant-status construction.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used Finnish PISA 2022 data. Overall model uses N=10,239 students. For immigrant-status multigroup models, immigrant status is computed from students’ country of birth and both parents’ information; if one of these questions is unanswered, the student receives no valid immigrant value, resulting in a reduced analytic sample (Ntotal=9,874; nonimmigrant=8,066; second-generation=790; first-generation=1,018).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (Finland) — overall model; achievement in Math (PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM mediation effects (standardized): ICT learning direct=0.014 (SE .017, n.s.); ICT learning total=0.084 (SE .018, p<.001). ICT leisure direct=-0.270 (SE .016, p<.001); ICT leisure total=-0.368 (SE .015, p<.001). Self-efficacy in CIL direct effect on Math: mediated path coefficient=0.115 (SE .010, p<.001). Self-efficacy in CT direct effect on Math: mediated path coefficient=-0.045 (SE .005, p<.001). Model fit: χ2=9937.020, RMSEA=.043, CFI=.930, TLI=.921, SRMR=.065.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Finland) overall model the study leveraged ICT use for learning, ICT use for leisure, self-efficacy in CIL, and self-efficacy in CT to predict Math achievement (PVs), finding that ICT use for learning had no significant direct effect but a positive total effect via mediation through self-efficacy in CIL, while ICT use for leisure showed a negative direct and total relationship with achievement. This indicates that promoting CIL-oriented digital self-efficacy may help translate learning-related ICT engagement into higher achievement, whereas leisure-oriented ICT use is associated with lower achievement, though the SEM is correlational and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (Finland) — overall model; achievement in Reading (PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM mediation effects (standardized): ICT learning direct=-0.018 (SE .018, n.s.); ICT learning total=0.050 (SE .020, p<.05). ICT leisure direct=-0.224 (SE .019, p<.001); ICT leisure total=-0.359 (SE .017, p<.001). Self-efficacy in CIL mediation coefficient=0.138 (SE .011, p<.001). Self-efficacy in CT mediation coefficient=-0.070 (SE .006, p<.001). Model fit: χ2=9937.020, RMSEA=.043, CFI=.930, TLI=.921, SRMR=.065.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Finland) overall model the study leveraged ICT use for learning, ICT use for leisure, self-efficacy in CIL, and self-efficacy in CT to predict Reading achievement (PVs), finding that ICT use for learning had no significant direct effect but a small positive total effect through mediation (positive via CIL and negative via CT), while ICT use for leisure had a negative direct and total relationship. This indicates that strengthening CIL self-efficacy may partially offset the achievement risks associated with ICT engagement, but leisure ICT use remains consistently associated with lower reading performance, with no causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (Finland) — overall model; achievement in Science (PVs)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM mediation effects (standardized): ICT learning direct=-0.004 (SE .020, n.s.); ICT learning total=0.065 (SE .021, p<.01). ICT leisure direct=-0.258 (SE .017, p<.001); ICT leisure total=-0.368 (SE .015, p<.001). Self-efficacy in CIL mediation coefficient=0.122 (SE .010, p<.001). Self-efficacy in CT mediation coefficient=-0.053 (SE .005, p<.001). Model fit: χ2=9937.020, RMSEA=.043, CFI=.930, TLI=.921, SRMR=.065.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Finland) overall model the study leveraged ICT use for learning, ICT use for leisure, self-efficacy in CIL, and self-efficacy in CT to predict Science achievement (PVs), finding that ICT use for learning showed no significant direct effect but a positive total effect via mediation through CIL self-efficacy, whereas ICT use for leisure had a negative direct and total relationship. This indicates that educational ICT policies should focus on building CIL-aligned competencies and self-efficacy rather than assuming that general ICT engagement will improve science outcomes.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 (Finland) — gender multigroup model; achievement in Math (PVs)
main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement (Plausible Values) — girls vs boys
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM mediation effects (standardized): Girls—ICT learning total=0.133 (SE .025, p<.001); ICT leisure total=-0.384 (SE .022, p<.001). Boys—ICT learning total=0.043 (SE .020, p<.05) and not significant for reading/science (as reported in text); ICT leisure total=-0.365 (SE .020, p<.001). Model fit: χ2=12043.011, RMSEA=.046, CFI=.918, TLI=.910, SRMR=.069.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 (Finland) gender multigroup model the study leveraged ICT use for learning, ICT use for leisure, self-efficacy in CIL, self-efficacy in CT, and gender to predict Math achievement (PVs), finding that ICT use for learning had a positive total effect for girls (and only a small positive effect for boys in math) while ICT use for leisure was negative for both groups. This indicates that gender-responsive support for CIL-oriented digital self-efficacy may be particularly important for translating learning-related ICT use into achievement gains for girls.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes Finnish PISA 2022 data (N=10,239 overall; immigrant-status groups Ntotal=9,874) to examine how ICT use and self-efficacy in digital competencies relate to achievement in math, reading, and science. The authors operationalize ICT use for learning (IC174) and ICT use for leisure (IC177), and split self-efficacy in digital competencies (IC183) into two latent factors: CIL (11 items) and CT (3 items). Using SEM in Mplus with Fay’s balanced repeated replication (BRR) and 10 plausible values per subject, they report acceptable model fit (overall: RMSEA=.043, CFI=.930, TLI=.921, SRMR=.065). Across subjects, ICT use for learning shows no significant direct effect but a positive total effect via mediation through CIL self-efficacy, whereas ICT use for leisure is negatively associated with achievement. The immigrant-status multigroup results suggest that CIL self-efficacy can be protective for immigrant students, but the paper does not fully document a general missing-data strategy beyond the immigrant-status derivation rule.
